content.thinking:
I need to structure the postmortem without inventing any figures myself, using placeholders wherever numbers would go. I'm outlining the causal chain starting with the drop in categorisation confidence and the small rise in error rate, tying each claim back to specific evidence citations like T6.

I'm working through whether the candidate's claim about the model version switch is actually confirmed by the logs — it isn't directly, so I should hedge it as an unverified assumption from the investigator rather than a confirmed fact, while noting the deploy timing coincided with onset and the rollback correlates with recovery. I'm also flagging a contributing factor: the alert was mislabeled as an error-rate alert when it was really tracking confidence, and it fired several minutes after the incident began.

For the write-up, I'll avoid any digits or version numbers like "v1"/"v2" and instead describe it as "the new model version," using the provided time placeholders instead of literal timestamps, and I'll number new action items (AI-3 through AI-5) covering detection delay, log review process gaps, and the pending fix PR. I'm now drafting the first step of the chain describing how categorisation confidence and error rates degraded between the incident's start and recovery.

Next I trace why: the service was running a new revision with lower-confidence categorisation answers, citing the deploy and metrics evidence to tie onset to the deployment minute. Then I link the revision change to a categoriser configuration update the investigator flagged in the diff, noting the rollback to the prior revision restored baseline behavior — and I'm careful to stop extending the causal chain where the evidence actually ends, since there's no gate or check confirmed in the record beyond the deploy itself. I land on a root cause statement: the new revision shipped a categoriser configuration with much lower confidence outputs, and no safeguard caught it before or during rollout, while flagging the model-change detail as the investigator's interpretation rather than confirmed fact.

action_items.item: Add a pre-release gate for categoriser changes. It should compare categorisation confidence on a fixed evaluation set against the current production version, and it should block or roll back a staged rollout when confidence falls well below the baseline.
Rename the CategorisationConfidenceLow alert so its title describes confidence rather than error rate. Review its evaluation window so that a sustained confidence drop pages sooner after onset.

Make the Investigator read the service's logs, including model and categoriser output, before it settles on a leading candidate. Record what it found so the cause is confirmed rather than inferred from metrics and the diff.

causal_chain.step: Users saw categorisation answers degrade between {began} and {recovered}. The confidence score the paging rule watches fell from {series_before} to {series_while_broken} on average and {series_at_worst} at worst, and the error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken}, peaking at {errors_at_worst}.
The replicas were answering with lower confidence because they were running a newly deployed revision. The drop began in the same minute that revision was deployed.

The new revision was the cause. Rolling back to the previous revision brought the service back to its baseline from {recovered}, and the paging rule stopped firing. The earlier deploy (P1) was hours before the onset, and the flag provider showed no recent flag changes, so neither explains the drop.

The revision reached production with a changed categoriser setting, read by the Investigator from the diff as a model version switch rather than an application code change. Its lower-confidence output was not caught before it served traffic. This was not confirmed from logs, because none were read. The evidence stops here.

contributing_factors.factor: No pre-release or canary check on categorisation quality. A model or configuration change could roll out to every replica with no confidence comparison against the previous version.

Slow detection. The alert was raised {alert_raised - began} after the onset. It was titled as an error-rate alert, though the series it evaluates is categorisation confidence, which is confusing for responders.
The investigation read no logs, so the cause of the confidence drop was not confirmed from the service's own output. The leading candidate rested on metrics and the change diff alone.
The fix to the underlying change is not yet merged, so the faulty change is still unresolved in the repository.

input.executive_summary: For {duration}, from {began} to {recovered}, the shop's product categorisation gave much less confident answers than normal. Requests were still served, and the failure rate rose only slightly, from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average, peaking at {errors_at_worst}. The cause was a deployment made at the start of the problem, which changed the categorisation model. Argus rolled the service back to the previous revision. Confidence returned to normal from {recovered}, and the rollback was confirmed. A draft fix has been proposed and is waiting for review. Argus held the incident for {held}, which measures the response, not the outage.

got_lucky: Requests kept being served, with only a small rise in errors and no latency impact, so the harm was limited to answer quality. A change that degraded quality this much could just as easily have gone unalerted for longer, because ordinary request metrics stayed near baseline.
went_well: Argus picked up the alert within seconds, and the Investigator placed the onset at the right minute and tied it to the deploy.
The rollback was applied quickly and confirmed from metrics. The service returned to baseline and the paging rule stopped firing.
A draft fix pull request was proposed straight after mitigation.
went_wrong: The faulty change reached every replica with no quality check, and users saw degraded categorisation until the rollback.
The alert came well after the onset and was labelled as an error-rate alert, though the signal is a confidence score.
No logs were read, so the cause rests on metrics and the diff.

input.root_cause: The deploy of revision 7c3ca00c7528df68d533f6e87acd4f23a55ab342 (P2) put a categoriser change into production, which the Investigator read from the diff as a switch to a new model version. After it, categorisation confidence fell sharply on every replica. Nothing checked categorisation quality before or during the rollout, so the change reached all replicas and was caught only by an alert after the fact.
input.symptom: Product categorisation became far less confident
